question_en: In a bankruptcy reorganization, which of the following categories of creditors is most likely to have the highest recovery rate?
explanation_en: Secured debt is backed by a claim (ie, lien) on specific assets pledged as collateral. Secured creditors have the most senior claim on the cash flows and assets of a company. As a type of secured debt, a second lien obligation is ranked ahead of all unsecured creditors and equity holders. Secured creditors' claims are paid first in any liquidation or obtain the highest recovery rates in a bankruptcy reorganization. In the case of a second lien obligation, first lienholders have a prior claim on the assets pledged as collateral. However, the collateral value is typically significantly greater than the original value of the claims of all lienholders. Should the collateral prove inadequate to cover the entire debt, secured creditors are ranked equally with senior unsecured creditors for the balance of their claims. (Choice B) Senior unsecured creditors are ranked ahead of all other unsecured creditors and all equity holders. However, senior unsecured creditors rank behind the secured creditors, including second and third lienholders, with respect to any asset pledged as collateral. (Choice C) Senior subordinated creditors are junior to the other listed creditor classes. Although senior to other subordinated creditors and equity holders, senior subordinated lenders have the lowest recovery rate among the categories of creditors shown here.

question_en: Which of the following ratios is most likely useful for an analyst comparing two retail companies?
explanation_en: Sales per square foot is commonly used in the retail industry and would serve as a good comparison. While growth in same-store sales may be useful to compare one company's different locations year-over-year (as it excludes any new locations), it would not be helpful for external comparisons. Sales per employee is generally used in service- or consultancy-based companies rather than retail.

subtopic: 7.06 Fixed-Income Bond Valuation Prices and Yields
question_en: An underwriter wants to estimate the offering price on a new issue for a 2-year bond with an 8.5% coupon rate that pays interest semiannually. The underwriter gathers comparative information on two publicly traded corporate bonds, Bonds Y and Z, with the same maturity and similar credit quality: The estimate of the new bond issue's price using matrix pricing is closest to:
explanation_en:
Matrix pricing can be used to approximate a new bond's issuance price from existing publicly traded bonds with a similar credit rating, maturity,
and/or coupon. In this question, the underwriter wants to derive the price of a new 2-year corporate bond from the characteristics of two similar
bonds. To derive the price, find the average periodic rate of the two publicly traded bonds, then use the rate to calculate the present value (ie,
price) of the new bond.
(Choice A) 103.7503 results from incorrectly approximating an average coupon payment for the new bond. The coupon payments of the new
bond are given in this scenario and should not be approximated.
(Choice B) 105.1310 results from treating the coupons as annual payments and discounting each payment at the stated annual coupon rate.

question_en: A hedge fund begins the year with £100 million in assets. The fund charges a 2% management fee and 20% incentive fee (calculated net of the management fee) on year-end assets, subject to a 6% hard hurdle rate. At year-end, the fund had appreciated by 8%. The investor's return is closest to:
explanation_en:
Typical hedge fund fee structure
Fee Basis for calculation Specific details
Typically 1%−3% of AUM annually
Assets under
Management Does not depend on fund's profitability
management (AUM)
Always calculated before incentive fee
Can be net or gross of management fee
Performance or incentive Annual returns Can be subject to hurdle rate and/or
high-water mark
A hedge fund investor's return is calculated net of fees and as a percentage of the fund's beginning-of-period value. Hedge funds often levy both a
management fee and an incentive fee.
The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the fund's total ending assets under management (AUM) and is assessed
regardless of profitability.
The incentive fee is calculated as a percentage of profits either net (ie, after deducting) or gross (ie, before deducting) of management
fees.
An incentive fee is often contingent on profits being greater than a hurdle rate and/or AUM being higher than a high-water mark. In this scenario,
the fund's threshold to earn an incentive fee is contingent on exceeding the 6% hard hurdle rate.
The investor's return for the year is calculated as follows:
(Choice A) 4.67% results from not accounting for the hurdle rate and assumes paying an incentive fee on £5.84 million.
(Choice C) 6.00% inappropriately assumes the management fee is calculated on beginning AUM, so that there are £2 million in total fees paid.

question_en: A fund of funds (FoF) has a "1 and 10" fee structure, with all fees calculated independently at year end. At the beginning of the year, the FoF has €150 million equally allocated among three hedge funds. For the year, the hedge fund's' returns are −2%, 10%, and 16%. If the FoF has a high-water mark of €152 million, the total fee paid to the FoF is closest to:
explanation_en:
Typical hedge fund fee structure
Fee Basis for calculation Specific details
Typically 1%−3% of AUM annually
Assets under
Management Does not depend on fund's profitability
management (AUM)
Always calculated before incentive fee
Can be net or gross of management fee
Performance or incentive Annual returns Can be subject to hurdle rate and/or
high-water mark
A fund of funds (FoF) is a hedge fund that invests in other hedge funds. Hedge funds often levy both a management fee and an incentive fee.
The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the fund's end-of-period assets under management (AUM) and is assessed
regardless of profitability.
The incentive fee is calculated as a percentage of profits either gross (ie, before deduction) or net (ie, after deduction) of management
fees.
If fees are calculated independently, calculations are on a gross basis.
An incentive fee is often contingent on profits being greater than a hurdle rate and/or the AUM being above a high-water mark (HWM), which is
the base asset value used to calculate the incentive fee. The HWM represents the fund's previous peak AUM value that has already earned an
incentive fee.
The FoF's fees and return are calculated (with year-end values and fees in € millions) as follows:
Steps Calculations
Calculate the FoF's year-end asset value 49 + 55 + 58 = 162
Calculate management fee 162 × 0.01 = 1.62
Calculate HWM-adjusted incentive fee base 162 − 152 = 10.0
Calculate incentive fee 10.0 × 0.10 = 1.00
Total fee paid to FoF 1.62 + 1.00 = 2.62
In this scenario, the total fee paid to the FoF is €2.62 million.
(Choice A) A total fee of €2.46 million results from calculating the incentive fee on a net basis.
(Choice B) A total of €2.50 million results from inappropriately using beginning AUM to calculate the management fee.

question_en: Conditions that most likely support a high weight of debt in a company's capital structure include:
option_c: having a high degree of operating leverage.
explanation_en: Because of the interest and principal obligations associated with debt financing, a company must be relatively stable to support the payments as they come due. Subscription-based revenue models, where customers pay monthly or annual recurring fees, are typically more predictable and stable than pay-per-use revenue models. Operating in a cyclical industry or with a high degree of operating leverage is more consistent with having a relatively low weight of debt in the capital structure.

question_en: Commodity price indexes are based on the prices of:
option_c: real assets such as grains, oil, and precious metals.
explanation_en: The constituent securities of commodity price indexes are commodity futures contracts. As a result, the return on a commodity index can be different than the returns from holding the constituent commodities themselves.

question_en: A researcher has data on the 20 largest firms in each state and samples the data by choosing 20 states at random and then selecting 10 firms at random from each of the samples. Her sampling method is referred to as:
explanation_en: The procedure described is an example of two-stage cluster sampling. With stratified random sampling, all subsets of the data (all states) would be included, and random samples would be selected from each. Convenience sampling is based on the low cost or easy availability of the data used.

subtopic: 7.07 Yield and Yield Spread Measures for Fixed-Rate Bonds
question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information on 10-year government benchmark rates (with YTMs assuming semiannual compounding):

| Benchmark | YTM |
|---|---|
| Government bond | 4.18% |
| Interest rate swap | 4.28% |
| Government spot rate | 4.35% |

For a 6% coupon semiannual pay corporate bond with 10 years to maturity and priced at 100.35, the g-spread in basis points (bps) is closest to:
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
Yield curves display the term structure of interest rates by graphing the relationship between maturities and bond yields. Many governments,
including those of the UK, US, and Japan, regularly issue bonds with select maturities (eg, 2, 5, 10, and 30 years). These benchmark bonds form
the basis of the government yield curve.
The g-spread is the difference between the YTM of a nongovernment bond relative to the YTM of a benchmark government bond with the
same maturity. It quantifies the additional yield (ie, spread) required by the market to own the riskier bond.
In this question, the YTM of the corporate bond can be derived from the information provided using a financial calculator. Stated on a semiannual
basis, the government bond's YTM is 4.18%, and the corporate bond's YTM is 5.95%. Therefore, the g-spread is 0.0595 − 0.0418 = 0.0177, or
177 bps.
(Choice A) 160 bps (0.0595 − 0.0435 = 0.0160) is the difference between the YTM of the bond and the spot rate. It results from an inappropriate
application of the Z-spread concept, which requires the entire benchmark curve's spot rates, not just a single period's YTM.
(Choice B) 167 bps (0.0595 − 0.0428 = 0.0167) is the difference between the YTM of the bond and the benchmark swap rate, or i-spread.

question_en: A bond's indenture least likely specifies the:
option_b: covenants that apply to the issuer.
explanation_en: The identity of the lender (i.e., the bondholder) is not specified in a bond's indenture because a bond may be traded during its life. An indenture or trust deed is a legal contract that specifies a bond issuer's obligations and restrictions. The indenture may include covenants that require the issuer to take or refrain from taking certain actions and may specify the source of funds for repayment, such as a project to be funded or the taxing power of a government.

question_en: The difference between the current ratio and the quick ratio is that the quick ratio excludes:
explanation_en: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities Quick ratio = (current assets – inventories) / current liabilities Marketable securities are included among current assets in both ratios. Neither ratio considers non-current assets.

subtopic: Reading 61 Curve-Based and Empirical Fixed-Income Risk Measures
question_en: The approach to estimating duration that relies on using historical relationships between benchmark yield changes and bond price changes is:
explanation_en: Empirical duration is estimated by using historical data between benchmark yield changes and bond price changes. Analytical duration approaches based on mathematical analysis include Macaulay, modified, and effective durations.

question_en: Fraud and malfeasance, soundness of strategy, and prior treatment of bondholders are criteria to evaluate a borrower's:
explanation_en: Character refers to the quality of management. Character analysis includes soundness of strategy, management's track record, accounting policies and tax strategies, fraud and malfeasance record, and prior treatment of bondholders. Capacity refers to the ability of the borrower to make its debt payments on time. Covenants are the terms and conditions of lending agreements with which the issuer must comply.

question_en: Which of the following risk metrics is most appropriate for measuring a bond's interest rate sensitivity?
explanation_en: Key risk management functions include measuring and monitoring risk. Quantifying risk allows a company to determine whether the expected benefits from a potential activity outweigh the costs and whether the activity's risk aligns with the company's risk guidelines. Certain measures are associated with specific asset classes. For example, duration is a measure of bond interest rate risk sensitivity. (Choice A) Measures of option risk are those that quantify the relationship between changes in the option's value and movements in the underlying's price and volatility such as delta, gamma, rho, and vega. (Choice B) Beta is most directly associated with equity securities and portfolios of equity securities. Beta measures an asset's sensitivity to market portfolio returns.

question_en: The time it takes for policy makers to determine that the economy requires a fiscal policy action is best described as:
explanation_en: Recognition lag refers to the time it takes for fiscal policy makers to determine the need for a policy action. Action lag is the time it takes policymakers to discuss, enact, and implement fiscal policy measures. Impact lag is the time it takes for a fiscal policy measure to have its effect on the economy.

question_en: The time it takes for a fiscal policy action to affect the economy is best described as:
explanation_en: The time it takes for a fiscal policy action, once implemented, to have its effect on the economy is referred to as impact lag. Recognition lag is the time it takes policymakers to realize a fiscal policy response is needed. Action lag is the time it takes policymakers to discuss, enact, and implement fiscal policy measures.

question_en: High risk tolerance, a long investment horizon, and low liquidity needs are most likely to characterize the investment needs of a(n):
explanation_en: A defined benefit pension plan typically has a long investment time horizon, low liquidity needs, and high risk tolerance. Insurance companies and banks typically have low risk tolerance and high liquidity needs. Banks and property and casualty insurers typically have short investment horizons.

question_en: An order to sell a security at the best price available is a:
explanation_en: A market order is an order to buy or sell a security immediately at the best available price. A limit order is an order to buy at the specified limit price or lower, or to sell at the limit price or higher. A stop order is an order to buy if the market price increases to the specified stop price, or to sell if the market price decreases to the stop price.

question_en: An investor purchases a bond with 5 years until maturity, a 4% annual coupon payment, and a YTM of 4.25%. The investor holds the bond until maturity. After purchase and before the first coupon, if the YTM for similar bonds increases to 4.5% due to a rise in interest rates and remains at that level for the life of the bond, then the value of the investor's reinvested coupons at maturity is closest to:
explanation_en:
Assuming no default, sources of return for a bond investor include:
coupon and principal payments received on the dates agreed upon in the contract;
interest on reinvestment (ie, interest on interest) of coupons between the time each one is received and the end of the bond's holding
period; and
capital losses or gains from any sale of the bond prior to maturity.
One assumption made in calculating the YTM is that the bond's coupon payments are reinvested at the YTM rate. However, that may not be
possible if interest rates change, which often happens (ie, interest rate risk). If so, the investor's rate of return will likely not be equal to the bond's
initial YTM.
A change in the YTM for similar bonds affects the rate at which the coupons can be reinvested. In this scenario, interest rates rise, which
increases the reinvestment rate. The future value of the reinvested coupons is calculated as follows:
Since interest rates have risen, the investor's reinvested coupons are worth $21.88 at maturity.
(Choice A) $21.67 is the value of the reinvested coupon if one incorrectly assumes that the coupons are reinvested at the coupon rate of 4%.
(Choice B) $21.77 results from assuming that the coupons are reinvested at the bond's YTM rate at purchase (ie, 4.25%).

question_en:
A manager is recommending portfolios to a $20 billion endowment fund. The manager is considering using one of the following portfolios:

| Portfolio Weights | Treasury Bills | Corporate Bonds | Common Stock | Venture Capital |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Portfolio X | 5% | 10% | 70% | 15% |
| Portfolio Y | 5% | 70% | 20% | 5% |
| Portfolio Z | 5% | 50% | 45% | 0% |

Based only on this information, which portfolio is most appropriate for the foundation?
explanation_en: An endowment is the investment portfolio of a nonprofit organization (NPO). Assets gifted to the NPO usually support its underlying cause over long periods of time. With its perpetual life (no end to the NPO), an endowment can withstand the high volatility of a risky investment. With its ability to tolerate higher risk, investors can expect to achieve greater returns. Investors can invest in the following broad asset types (in order of risk): Cash (eg, Treasury bills, certificates of deposit) Bonds (eg, fixed-income securities, corporate bonds, foreign government bonds) Stocks (eg, domestic, foreign) Alternatives (eg, venture capital, hedge funds) Venture capital (VC), a type of alternative investment, is one of the riskiest investments. An endowment complements its long-time horizons with risky investments because it can withstand short-term underperformance. Portfolio X is the best choice due to its highest allocation to VC (15%) and common stocks (70%). (Choice B) Portfolio Y, with the highest allocation to corporate bonds (70%), is the most conservative and least risky portfolio despite having a small allocation to VC. This allocation is suboptimal for an investor who has a high threshold for tolerating risk. (Choice C) This moderate portfolio has less allocation to bonds and more to common stocks than Portfolio Y but has no allocation to VC. Although it is more aggressive than Portfolio Y, it is more appropriate for an investor with lower risk tolerance than an endowment.

subtopic: Reading 50 Fixed-Income Cash Flows and Types
question_en: A bond initially does not make periodic payments but instead accrues them over a pre- determined period and then pays a lump sum at the end of that period. The bond subsequently makes regular periodic payments until maturity. Such a bond is best described as a:
explanation_en: Deferred-coupon bonds carry coupons, but the initial coupon payments are deferred for some period. The coupon payments accrue, at a compound rate, over the deferral period and are paid as a lump sum at the end of that period. After the initial deferment period has passed, these bonds pay regular coupon interest for the rest of the life of the issue (i.e., until the maturity date). Zero coupon bonds do not pay periodic interest. A step-up note has a coupon rate that increases on one or more specified dates during the note's life.

question_en: An organization is concerned it will be unable to continue to operate because it has run out of cash. This is an example of:
explanation_en: Solvency risk is the risk that an organization will not be able to operate because it ran out of cash. Credit risk is the risk that a counterparty will not fulfill its contractual obligations. Liquidity risk is the risk that an asset will be sold at a loss at a price below the asset's underlying fair value due to the market conditions at the time of the sale.

subtopic: 8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives
question_en: Which of the following is least likely to affect the value of a derivative instrument relative to the price of the underlying asset?
option_c: Expected rate of return on the underlying asset
explanation_en: Derivative pricing concepts Traders take advantage of any mispricing of derivatives Riskless strategies are created from offsetting positions in Arbitrage-free derivatives and underlying assets Strategies are pursued until risk-free profits are eliminated (ie, no-arbitrage pricing) Derivatives can be created synthetically from underlying and Replication risk-free assets Equivalent positions must have the same expected returns Derivative price reflects the value of the replicating strategy Riskless positions are created from long/short derivatives Risk-neutral and replication strategies Riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return; cash flows are discounted at the risk-free rate Replication and arbitrage are the foundations of derivative pricing. Investors can replicate assets by combining positions in derivatives and the risk-free asset. Economically equivalent positions should trade at prices that result in equal returns. If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer be earned. Therefore, derivatives trade at arbitrage-free prices. Under these pricing conditions, investors can create riskless positions (eg, long stock index and short stock index futures), which earn a risk-free rate of return. The ability to create riskless positions and arbitrage-free pricing means that risk aversion has no role in derivative pricing. Therefore, investor risk neutrality is assumed in derivative pricing. (Choice B) Since a long or short position in derivatives is not risk free, its expected returns would not be equal to the risk-free rate. Risk-free securities (eg, government T-bills) have expected returns equal to the risk-free rate. (Choice C) Derivatives can trade at either a discount or premium to the underlying and still be fairly valued. Any difference between underlying and derivative prices reflects cost of carry arbitrage pricing, not an adjustment for the relative riskiness.

question_en: The EUR/GBP spot exchange rate is 1.1650. The EUR one-year interest rate is 0.25%, and the GBP one-year interest rate is 1.50%. The one- year forward exchange rate expressed in forward points is closest to:
explanation_en: Exchange rate quotes specify the amount of one currency to be traded for one unit of another currency. The value is expressed in units of the price currency per one unit of the base currency. If the EUR/GBP exchange rate is quoted at 1.1650, it costs 1.1650 EUR (the price currency) to purchase one GBP (the base currency). The spot exchange rate is the value at which one currency can be traded for another today. The forward exchange rate is the current quotation for the value at which one currency can be exchanged for another in the future. The difference between the spot and forward exchange rates is determined by the relative level of risk-free interest rates in the two currencies. Given the spot rate and one-year interest rates in the two currencies, the one-year forward rate can be calculated. The forward points equal forward exchange rate minus the spot exchange rate, with the difference multiplied by 10,000 (unless the JPY is one of the currency pair, in which case the multiplier is 100). (Choice B) −115 is the negative of the one-year forward exchange rate. (Choice C) 145 is the result if the EUR and GBP interest rates are inverted in the forward exchange rate calculation.

question_en: A large company with a low credit rating needs to borrow a large amount of money. If the company operates in a country with an underdeveloped bond market, which of the following is the company's most likely source of funds?
explanation_en: Bank loans are the primary source of debt financing for small- and medium-size companies. Large companies may also use bank loans instead of issuing bonds if the company: is in an underdeveloped bond market area; must compete for bond issuance in a market where government entities and financial institutions dominate ("crowd out") corporate issuers; or has a low credit rating, making bond issuance more expensive than a bank loan. A syndicated loan is made by a group (ie, syndicate) of financial institutions (eg, banks, insurance companies, and other lenders) to a single borrower. A syndicated loan is appropriate when no single lender wishes to make a bilateral loan (ie, single lender to single borrower) and take on all the credit risk of the loan (Choice A). A substantial loan to a large company with a low credit rating, as described in this case, would involve high credit risk, making a syndicate a more likely source of funds than a single lender. (Choice B) Large, established companies with high credit ratings issue bonds perceived as relatively safe investments by bond markets. For such companies, issuing bonds may be less expensive, and therefore more desirable, than taking out bank loans. The exceptions to this general rule is when bond markets are not fully developed or when government entities "crowd out" private companies in bond issuance.
